messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Thompson is a 68-year-old African widower who has been a dancer for most of his life. His world changed dramatically when he was involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that left him feeling profoundly unsafe and uncertain about the future. Since the accident, Mr. Thompson’s days are marked by an overwhelming sense of dread and an unshakable belief that he cannot fully trust himself or the world around him. The traumatic event itself was a turning point for Mr. Thompson, but it is the fragments of memory that haunt him most. He struggles to piece together a coherent narrative of what happened on that fateful day. Instead, his mind conjures bits and pieces—sudden flashes of pain, the sound of shattering glass—and leaves gaping holes in between. This fragmented recollection has led Mr. Thompson to doubt not only the reliability of his memories but also the trustworthiness of his own body. He often feels like he can’t control what happens next and wonders if he will ever be able to do the right thing again. Mr. Thompson’s self-doubt is pervasive, and it manifests in how he navigates daily life. He has come to believe that his body no longer serves him reliably, which exacerbates his sense of vulnerability. This profound lack of trust in himself and others has led Mr. Thompson to avoid going out and socializing with friends from before the event. Even within the confines of his home, he feels safest when his back is against a wall where he can see everything happening around him. The fear that something bad will happen if things take longer than expected has made simple tasks like grocery shopping nearly impossible for Mr. Thompson. He becomes highly alert to unexpected or loud sounds and interprets them as signs of impending danger. This heightened state of vigilance is exhausting, and it makes every moment feel precarious. For instance, he finds himself unable to relax even when sitting in his favorite chair at home, always waiting for the next sound that could signal a threat. These persistent fears are not just abstract worries; they have practical consequences. Mr. Thompson has stopped dancing altogether, which was once his passion and livelihood. He no longer feels safe performing in front of others or trusting his body to execute the precise movements he once mastered. Instead, he confines himself to the safety of his home, where he can control most aspects of his environment. Mr. Thompson’s avoidance behaviors have further deepened his sense of isolation and mistrust. Each time he avoids going out or seeing friends, it reinforces the belief that external threats are omnipresent and that institutions meant to protect him have let him down. This vicious cycle has made it increasingly difficult for Mr. Thompson to engage in any activity outside the comfort of his home. What frightened Mr. Thompson most was the realization that his once-reliable body now betrayed him, leaving him feeling helpless and exposed. He had come to believe that every unexpected sound or delay could mean harm was imminent. This constant threat monitoring has led him to avoid anything that might trigger these fears, including therapy sessions where he would be prompted to discuss and reflect on the traumatic event. It was this growing isolation and the persistent fear of re-experiencing the trauma in any form that finally brought Mr. Thompson to seek help. He is most hopeful for a return to a sense of control over his body and mind, and a way to piece together the fragmented memories so that he can move forward with a clearer understanding of what happened. Mr. Thompson’s current state is one of profound uncertainty and fear, but there is also an underlying desire to reclaim some semblance of normalcy in his life. He is most afraid of being trapped in this cycle indefinitely, unable to trust himself or the world around him again. Yet, he remains hopeful that through therapy, he can find a path toward healing and rediscovering the confidence he once had as both a dancer and an individual capable of navigating daily life with safety and assurance.
